$schema_note: AUTHORED, and deliberately small. One entry per platted block claimed from the 665-roof programme's schedule (data/reconstruction/1835_665_roof_programme.json, derived by tools/reconcile_665.py). Expanded into ordinary one-file-per-structure records by tools/generate_block_infill.py, which tools/check.sh re-derives. This file authors NO coordinates: every metre comes from the committed lot polygons in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and every dimension from the family bands in 1835_family_archetype_crosswalk.json. What is authored here is which family stands on which lot, whether it fronts the street or the alley, and how far back it stands.
why_the_schedule_is_copied_here: The schedule is DERIVED from what stands, so a block's family mix is erased the moment the block is built — it becomes at_capacity with no mix at all. A generator reading the live schedule would therefore write ten records on its first run and none on its second, and the re-derivation gate would fail on the commit that shipped it. `drawn_from_schedule` and `families` are the claim a parcel made against the schedule at the moment it claimed it, frozen so the expansion stays reproducible. tools/generate_block_infill.py checks the slots against them; tools/reconcile_665.py re-derives the schedule from the result.

placement_rule.principal: One principal roof per lot, standing back from its own street frontage, its facade to the street and its walls parallel to the block face. The setback is a period typology and not a measurement of this lot.
placement_rule.ancillary: A yard building off the block alley, behind a principal roof on the same lot, facing the alley.
placement_rule.open_lots: Alternating open lots are intentional and are what the phase-one parcel already assumes. A block at capacity is a claim about 1835 that the evidence does not support; the schedule's capacity is a ceiling.
placement_rule.what_is_invented: All of it. Which family stands where, which lot is left open, the setbacks and the lateral offsets are inventions bounded by the programme, not readings of a source. No lot is numbered: this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet, and the side lot lines and the alley are conjectural even where the block face is not.

blocks.arrangement_note: The block stood empty. Seven of its eight lots take a principal roof and the eighth is left open. The two larger houses take Randolph, which is the through street of the pair, and the rougher dwellings take Washington: that is a typology of frontage value, argued from the street hierarchy the plat module measures, and it is not evidence about this block. The three yard buildings serve the lots they stand behind — a stable behind the merchant's house because that is the household with a horse, a privy behind the other Randolph house, a woodshed behind the log dwelling on Washington. Each of those is a reason for the roof, not evidence for it.

open_lot.why: A south-tier interior lot, left open so the block does not read as a completed terrace. Which lot is arbitrary within the block; that one is open at all is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy.

deferred.why: The schedule deals this block one civic or public-service roof and the parcel refuses it rather than massing it. I3 resolves through the fort_structure placeholder, whose entire vocabulary of building kinds is garrison words — quarters, barracks, blockhouse, magazine, store, guard, sutler, artillery — and none of them names the adapted office or the engine house the crosswalk says this family spans. Massing an anonymous town civic building through that archetype would not merely guess at a function; it would stand a garrison building in the middle of the platted town, three quarters of a kilometre from the fort. The crosswalk already states the precondition on its own entry: the six-roof aggregate spans unlike functions and they must reconcile to named public records before construction is selected. A dwelling nobody named is the ordinary case in this town; a public building nobody named is a claim that an institution existed and left no record, and the two are not the same kind of anonymity.

blocks.arrangement_note: The easternmost block the plat module covers on the Randolph tier, bounded by Randolph, State, Washington and Dearborn, and empty in this dataset before this parcel. The schedule dealt it ten roofs and no house or commercial family at all — five dwellings across the rough end of the range, four yard buildings and the civic roof this parcel defers. Five principal roofs on eight lots leaves three lots open. What is argued here and not found: the three better-built dwellings (the deep-plan and two-room cottages and the one-room cottage) take the Randolph face because Randolph is the through street of the pair in the module's own street hierarchy, which is the same frontage-value typology the Randolph and Wells block recorded, and the log cabin and the plank shanty take Washington. The four yard buildings each stand behind a principal roof on its own lot, because a rear yard belongs to a lot and a lot belongs to a house. The barn or carriage shed takes the eastern end lot, where the block backs onto ground the plat module does not reach and the town gives out; that is a typology of where a town keeps a large animal shelter, not evidence about this block.

open_lots.why: A north-tier interior lot on the Randolph face, left open. Which lot is arbitrary within the tier; that a block this far east of the river is not a completed terrace is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy, and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target.

A south-tier lot the schedule left nothing to stand on once the civic roof was deferred. It is open because the parcel refused a slot, and the record of why is in `deferred` rather than in an argument about vacancy.
A south-tier interior lot, left open on the same alternating-vacancy assumption as lot 4.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first West Division block this module reaches, bounded by Randolph, Canal, Washington and Clinton, and the first block off the reconciled schedule that was NOT empty when the parcel arrived. Three anonymous roofs from the pre-plat West approaches parcel already stand inside it — recon_1835_west_018, _019 and _021, placed from typed coordinates months before the plat module existed, so no record of theirs names a lot. The generator now derives which lots they hold from their own committed footprints rather than being told, and refuses a principal roof on any of them; the schedule's headroom of seven is the block's headroom and never a licence to stand a second house on an occupied lot. That leaves five free lots for the four principal roofs the schedule deals, and one is left open. What is argued here and not found: the deep-plan and two-room cottages take the Randolph face, because Randolph is the through street of the pair in the module's own street hierarchy and carries the crossing to the west side, which is the same frontage-value typology both Randolph-tier blocks before this one recorded; the log dwelling and the one-room cottage take Washington. The barn or carriage shed takes the western end lot, where the block backs onto ground beyond Clinton that has no committed street control and the town gives out — the same typology of where a town keeps a large animal shelter that the Randolph and Dearborn block applied at its eastern end, and the geography here reverses it, which is the test of whether it was a typology or a habit. The stable and the privy stand behind the cottages on their own lots. None of it is evidence about this block.

open_lots.why: A south-tier interior lot between an already-built lot and the Washington end lot, left open. Which lot is arbitrary within the tier; that a West Division block a bridge's distance from the business street is not a completed terrace is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy, and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first South Division block of the Randolph row, bounded by Randolph, Franklin, Washington and Market, and the first block off the schedule whose standing roofs were put there by THIS project's own inferred-household layer rather than by a pre-plat coordinate parcel. inf_sawyer_dwelling_a and _b hold lots 4 and 6 — the two sawyer households of the occupation census, placed from typed coordinates before the plat module existed — so the block arrives with its Randolph face half built and both remaining free lots on that face. That is what decides the arrangement: the through street fills first, and the vacancy the programme requires has nowhere to fall but the Washington face. What is argued here and not found: the deep-plan and the one-and-a-half-storey cottages take the two free Randolph lots, because Randolph is the through street of the pair in the module's own street hierarchy and carries the west-side crossing — the same frontage-value typology the three Randolph-tier blocks before this one recorded. The two-room and the one-room cottages take Washington, the back street. Lots 1 and 5 are left open in alternation with them, and lot 1 is the one named first because it is the Washington-and-Market corner: Market is the river edge of the South Division here, and the corner nearest the wharves and the lumber ground is the least attractive residential lot on the block. The barn or carriage shed takes lot 7, the Franklin end of the quiet street and the furthest point on the block from the Randolph-and-Market bridge approach — the same where-a-town-keeps-a-large-animal-shelter typology the two blocks before this one applied at their own quiet ends, tested here against a third geometry rather than repeated. The stable, the woodshed and the privy stand behind the cottages on their own lots. None of it is evidence about this block, and no lot is numbered.

open_lots.why: The Washington-and-Market corner lot, left open. Market Street is the river edge of the South Division at this latitude and the ground beyond it is wharf and lumber ground, so the corner where the back street meets it is the least attractive residential lot the block has. Which lot is arbitrary within the tier; that a block one street back from the business front is not a completed terrace is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy, and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target.

A Washington-tier interior lot, left open in alternation with the two this parcel builds on, which is the pattern the phase-one parcel already assumes and the only face of this block with room left to express it: the Randolph face arrived with two of its four lots already carrying a roof and the schedule's headroom fills the other two.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first block off the South Water row, bounded by South Water, Wells, Lake and Franklin, and the first block this lane has taken on the town's BUSINESS front rather than one street back from it. It arrives with three roofs standing and none of them anonymous: the Temple Building holds lot 0 at the South Water and Franklin corner, the Exchange Coffee House holds lot 7 at the Lake and Wells corner, and J. H. Kinzie's forwarding store laps the north edge of lot 2 without taking any of its buildable part (T-A7 measured that at 9.7 m², all of it in the 1.5 m margin strip). What is argued here and not found: South Water is the valuable frontage of the pair — it is the river street, it carries every documented commercial roof near this block, and the module's own street hierarchy ranks it above Lake — so the three deepest dwellings the schedule deals take its three free lots, and the two meanest take Lake, the back street. Within each face the better roof stands nearer Wells, because Wells is the town-centre end of this block and Franklin the lumber-and-wharf end: the deep-plan cottage takes lot 6, the two-room lot 4 and the one-room lot 2, and on Lake the log cabin takes lot 5 against the shanty on lot 3. The one-room cottage is also the smallest of the three principal roofs the South Water face gets, which is the arrangement that leaves Kinzie's lap the most room — but the lap did NOT constrain the block, and saying so is the point of measuring it: lot 2's roof stands 7.3 m from that store against a 3 m separation gate, and every other roof this parcel places is further from its own nearest neighbour than that. The half-metre of extra setback on lot 2 was authored with the lap in view and turned out not to be needed. A reader should not have to re-measure to find out whether the standing commercial roofs squeezed this block; they did not. The stable takes the yard of lot 3 — the quiet street's far end once the Lake and Franklin corner is left open — which is the same where-a-town-keeps-a-large-animal-shelter typology the three blocks before this one applied at their own quiet ends, tested here against a fourth geometry rather than repeated. The privy stands behind the two-room cottage on lot 4. None of it is evidence about this block, and no lot is numbered.

open_lots.why: The Lake-and-Franklin corner, left open. Franklin is the lumber-and-wharf end of this block and Lake is its back street, so the corner where the two meet is the least attractive residential lot the block has — the same tier reasoning the Randolph and Market parcel applied to its own back-street corner. Which lot within the tier is arbitrary; that a block on the business front is not a completed terrace one street back is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy, and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target.
